extracted.intended_audience: practical geometers / surveyors / students learning measurement techniques
extracted.subtask_description: Practical/technical instructions for measuring distances, heights, areas, and volumes in the field using simple instruments (rule/gnomon/quadrant, plumb, rope, mirror, shadow). Contains procedural rules, proportional-scaling methods, and worked numeric examples for surveying problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instrument placement and fixing
rubrics_metrics.description: Place the measuring instrument (regola/gnomo/quad rante) exactly at the specified point and fix it so it cannot move during the observation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure the instrument is firmly set at the point to be measured (locbio tuo nel ponto), put the rule/gnomon along the intended side or direction, and keep it steady while sighting; if anything obstructs the view or the instrument slips the measurement will be invalid. Note any impediment and adjust placement before recording.

rubrics_metrics.name: Check for impediments before measuring
rubrics_metrics.description: Before taking a measurement, look along the line of sight and verify there is no obstacle that hides or disturbs the sight of the target point.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an impediment is seen on the line or part of the side, note which part is obstructed and either move the instrument or choose another point so the line of sight is clear (guarda ... se nulla impedimento).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of plumb (filo) for vertical alignment
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a plumb line to ensure vertical alignment of the instrument and to transfer/mark vertical points on the plane.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Let the plumb hang and note where it falls on the instrument or line; when the plumb corresponds to the correct mark the instrument is properly aligned. Use the plumb to mark points (ponilo tuo ilrumento ... il filo caggia) and to ensure the instrument won't be moved while sighting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Divide instrument scale into convenient integer parts
rubrics_metrics.description: When using proportional methods, divide the instrument's scale or the reference segment into whole integer parts (e.g., 24, 36, 40, 60, 120, 240) to facilitate multiplication and avoid fractional arithmetic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer numbers with many divisors (24, 36, 40, 60, 120, 240) so that proportions reduce to smaller whole numbers. The text repeatedly demonstrates choosing such partitions and multiplying/dividing by them to get whole-number results (esempi: 24, 36, 40, 60, 240, 360).

rubrics_metrics.name: Measuring linear distances on a plane by proportional transfer
rubrics_metrics.description: To measure the distance between two points on a plane, place the instrument at a known point, mark off proportional divisions on a line (using the instrument's scale), and transfer those divisions to obtain the desired segment by multiplicative proportions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedure: put the instrument at point A, align to B, mark the scale divisions (e.g., 24 or 36 parts), then count and transfer the number of parts corresponding to the required ratio. Numerous worked numeric examples show taking a base partition and multiplying/dividing to reach the target number of points (e.g., divide into 240 parts, take 36 parts, multiply/divide to reconstruct distance).

rubrics_metrics.name: Using the quadrant with plumb to measure height
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a quadrant (with a plumb line) placed at an appropriate point so that the plumb crosses a marked arc; read the arc or use the proportional relation between the instrument reading and the base distances to compute the height.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Place the quadrant on the chosen side/line, let the plumb indicate the arc point, and either read off angular measure or use the constructed proportional divisions to compute height by multiplication/division. The manual gives many arithmetic examples showing how to multiply the observed parts to recover the true height (e.g., use 60/240 partitions and scale up).

rubrics_metrics.name: Shadow (ombra) method for height determination
rubrics_metrics.description: Measure the shadow of the unknown-height object and the shadow of a reference object (or gnomon). Use similarity of triangles (proportions) between heights and shadows to compute the unknown height.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Place the gnomon or reference upright, measure its shadow and the tower/tree shadow at the same time; set up proportions (height_ref : shadow_ref = height_target : shadow_target) and solve by multiplication/division. The text describes picking times and arranging the instrument to observe shadows and then composing proportions and integer multipliers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mirror (specchio) method for height
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a mirror laid on the plane so that when the observer sees the top of the object in the mirror, distances from observer and object to the mirror relate by equal angles and similar triangles; measure those distances to compute height.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Place the mirror on the ground and move the observer until the top is seen; measure the distances from the mirror to the observer and to the target base, then use proportional relations to find the height. The manual instructs how to place and measure via the mirror and then multiply the measured segments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Using multiple observation points and integer scaling to determine inaccessible heights
rubrics_metrics.description: When the direct measurement is infeasible, take observations from multiple points at known multiples of a base distance; use integer multipliers and proportional arithmetic to infer the height.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: take measurements at 1×, 2×, 4× distances (or partitions like 24, 36, 40, 60), record the instrument readings at each, then multiply/divide according to the chosen common partition to arrive at the actual height. This reduces fractional work and error accumulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measuring across obstacles (rivers, mountains) by sightline and rope
rubrics_metrics.description: To measure the width of a river or distance across an obstacle, stretch a rope or mark a line from the tower top or reference to the near bank, measure along that line and use the proportional relation between the rope length and the tower height/line-of-sight to compute the width.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedure illustrated: fix a rope from the tower top to the bank, measure the rope length and the projection on the plane, choose integer multiples to square or scale (examples: multiply by 40 or 2500 etc.), subtract to get square/difference as needed, and extract the width via proportional arithmetic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measuring circular quantities: diameter, circumference and related areas
rubrics_metrics.description: Use relations between a circle's diameter, its circumference, and areas to compute areas/perimeters by proportional scaling (e.g., forming squares from diameters, using roots and multipliers).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text prescribes constructing squares from diameters or using perpendiculars from contact points to center to locate diameters; it shows numeric multipliers (e.g., multiply diameter by itself and by factors such as 64, 75, 88 in examples) to compute circumferential lengths and surface areas of circular bases and related solids (barrels, padiglioni, pyramids).

rubrics_metrics.name: Perpendicular from tangent/contact to circle center for construction
rubrics_metrics.description: When a polygon side is tangent to a circle, the line from the point of contact to the center is perpendicular to the side; use this to locate centers, diameters, or to construct perpendiculars for measurements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedure: draw the line from the contact point into the circle to the center; that line is perpendicular to the tangent side. Use this fact to drop perpendiculars and to divide arcs or to relate polygon sides to the circle's diameter for area computations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compute areas and contents of barrels/pyramids/containers by scaling
rubrics_metrics.description: To find the capacity (volume) of barrels, pyramids, tuns, etc., relate cross-sectional areas (or base areas) and heights by proportional multiplication; multiply relevant diameters/areas by prescribed numeric factors to get volumes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples given: treat a barrel or a pyramid as composed of proportional parts; multiply the base area by certain integers (examples in the text: factors like 4, 16, 36, 64, etc.) and combine to reach the content measure (braccia, barili). The manual uses many worked numeric scalings and partitions to convert between surface/area and body contents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Divide a segment into equal parts using instrument subdivisions
rubrics_metrics.description: To transfer proportions, divide your reference segment on the instrument into equal points (e.g., 24, 36, 40, 60), then use those points to proportionally construct or measure other segments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mark the equal points on the rule/scale (ex.: 24, 36, 60) and use them repeatedly; to produce a segment proportional to a given ratio, count off the corresponding number of points and transfer them. Many worked examples show transferring 24/36/40-part partitions and multiplying/dividing them to obtain desired segments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer integer arithmetic and reduce to fewer operations
rubrics_metrics.description: Arrange the measurement and the chosen partitions so that multiplications and divisions produce whole numbers as far as possible, minimizing fractional operations which increase error.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text repeatedly advises choosing partitions and multipliers (120, 240, 360, 400, 500, etc.) to get integer results and then performing multiplications/divisions in sequence; it gives worked examples where choosing different partitions simplifies the arithmetic (anti-pattern: choosing awkward numbers that create many fractional remainders).

rubrics_metrics.name: Record and mark measured points meticulously
rubrics_metrics.description: While measuring, mark points on lines and note counts (number of 'ponti' or divisions), because the subsequent computations depend on these recorded divisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mark each counted point (ponga il segno, poni la regola, nota il punto) and keep track of how many subdivisions are used; use these marks to place the instrument again or to transfer proportions. The manual shows step-by-step marking of points, removal of instrument, and subsequent line drawing from those marks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measuring depths and unattainable lower parts via angle/proportion
rubrics_metrics.description: To measure a depth (e.g., well mouth, lower part not visible), use an angle sight and proportional relations from an accessible point and scale with integer partitions to compute the depth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Place instrument at a visible rim point, sight to the bottom point (or its reflection/shadow), measure the corresponding divisions, and compute the depth by multiplying/dividing using chosen partition factors; use the same precautions about plumb and impediments.
